r674: For a long time many people believed the adult brain stopped changing. Research now shows the brain keeps forming new connections throughout life, a quality called neuroplasticity. Learning a language and a musical instrument are among the more demanding activities for the brain, using memory, hearing, movement and attention together. Studies suggest that such learning, along with exercise, social connection and good sleep, may help support thinking skills as we age. Wilfred's dullness was partly due to too little challenge and too little connection. His brain needed new problems to solve and people to share them with.
r675: One morning he played "How Great Thou Art" all the way through without stopping. His wife clapped from the kitchen. Wilfred realised his brain was not finished, and that God still had growth planned for him.

r682: Caleb at eighty-five said, "As yet I am as strong this day as I was in the day that Moses sent me" (Joshua 14:11), and he asked for a new mountain to take. Scripture promises that the righteous "shall still bring forth fruit in old age" (Psalm 92:14). Paul wrote, "though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day" (2 Corinthians 4:16). The psalmist sang, "I will sing unto the LORD as long as I live" (Psalm 104:33). God's people are invited to keep growing, praising and learning to the very end.
r683: God designed the brain to keep growing. Each time Wilfred practised, neurons that fired together strengthened their connections, and repeated practice may help pathways become faster and more efficient. Challenge, curiosity and joy all seem to support this growth. God also designed us for community, so learning alongside others adds motivation and meaning. Ageing brings real changes, but it does not end the capacity to learn. Our Creator made us to remain learners, growing in wisdom and skill throughout life.

r688: After a year Wilfred could hold simple conversations in German and played keyboard at the Sunday evening service, making mistakes that people kindly overlooked. Some weeks his arthritis made practice painful, and he had to slow down. His memory did not become perfect, but he felt sharper and happier. He now encourages other retirees at church to start something new.
r689: The brain can keep learning and growing at any age when we give it new challenges, practice and community.

r791: Scripture shows that God settles a leader's identity before He sends them to lead. In John 13:3-4 we read that "Jesus knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands" rose from supper and took a towel. He knew who He was, so He could kneel and wash feet without feeling small. When David's own men spoke of stoning him, 1 Samuel 30:6 says he "encouraged himself in the LORD his God." Psalm 62:5-7 calls God our rock and our glory, and Galatians 1:10 reminds us that a servant of Christ does not live to please men. Noticing the sting, naming your worth in God and then asking Him for wisdom follows this pattern. You lead from what God has already said about you, not from what people give or withhold.
r792: When someone ignores or disrespects you, research suggests the brain treats it as a social threat. The amygdala signals alarm, stress hormones such as cortisol and adrenaline rise, the heart speeds up and the body gets ready to defend itself. In that state the prefrontal cortex, the part behind your forehead that plans and weighs choices, works less well, so we tend to snap, sulk or give up. Naming the sting calms the alarm a little, because putting feelings into words seems to quiet the amygdala. Saying a truth about your worth and separating the person from the problem brings the thinking brain back online. Practised over weeks, these steps build a quicker pathway from hurt to calm, so you react less and choose one wise action more often.
r793: God made us to receive our worth before we do our work. Adam was blessed before he had planted a single garden, and Jesus heard the Father say He was beloved before His ministry began. This order matters because a leader who needs approval will either control people or be controlled by them. God, who is secure and unshaken in Himself, wants His children to share that security. He designed the brain so that a settled sense of belonging lowers threat and frees our minds to think, plan and love. When your worth rests in Him, a disobedient child, a stubborn team member or a cold church member cannot take it away. You become free to correct gently, wait patiently and keep serving, which is how God Himself leads us.
r794: Jesus gave a clear and gentle way to deal with wrongs. In Matthew 18:15 He said, "If thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone." He did not tell us to shame people in public or to stay silent and bitter. Galatians 6:1 asks us to restore others in a spirit of meekness, Proverbs 27:5-6 says open rebuke is better than secret love, and Ephesians 4:15 tells us to speak the truth in love. A private meeting, a specific description of the problem, honest listening, a clear expectation and a kind follow-up all follow this teaching. If nothing changes, involving one or two others or the proper process is exactly the next step Jesus described.
r795: In studies, people who feel publicly shamed show a strong threat response, with the amygdala firing and the body flooding with stress hormones. When that happens they defend themselves rather than listen. Meeting privately and at a calm time lowers this alarm for both of you. Describing one specific behaviour and its effect is easier for the brain to process than a vague attack on someone's character, so the other person's prefrontal cortex can stay engaged. Asking their side and listening helps them feel heard, which research links to more trust and cooperation. A clear expectation removes the guessing that often looks like disrespect. Over several weeks, repeated calm conversations teach both your nervous systems that correction can be safe, and the relationship begins to feel steadier.
r796: God Himself corrects us in this way. He does not humiliate His children, but He speaks to us personally, names what is wrong and invites us back. Think of how Jesus spoke privately with Peter by the lakeshore after his denial, asking honest questions and giving him a clear calling again. God designed us so that truth spoken with love can be received, while truth thrown in anger is usually rejected. He holds both justice and mercy together, and the respect conversation reflects both. It takes the wrong seriously and also takes the person seriously. This is how families, churches and teams can grow without fear. You are joining God's own patient way of shaping people, which aims not at winning an argument but at restoring a relationship.
